canonical_topic: Node, zone, and hub pricing under SMD
definition: Under the Standard Market Design (SMD), power prices are calculated at three levels of granularity: nodes (specific physical delivery points), zones (geographic aggregations of nodes), and hubs (aggregations of selected nodes across multiple zones).
core_idea: The systemwide power clearing price is the same everywhere, but congestion and line-loss charges vary by location, so nodal, zonal, and hub prices diverge from each other and from the clearing price depending on where you sit on the grid.
key_points: Node price = price at a specific electrical bus (interface where power enters/leaves the transmission grid); generators are paid the nodal price at their delivery point.
Zone price = average of all nodal prices within a defined geographic area; used for buyers/customers because it requires less detailed metering.
Hub price = average of selected nodal prices spanning several zones; serves as the grid's benchmark price and is the price used extensively in forward market trading.
In most ISO/RTO regions the systemwide clearing price and the hub price are treated as synonymous.
relationships: Node/zone/hub pricing is the basis for Financial Transmission Rights (FTRs), which hedge the price difference between hub and node.
Hub prices anchor forward market contracts.
trading_implications: A generator's realized revenue is its nodal price, which can differ materially from the hub price traders use for forward hedges — creating basis risk that FTRs are designed to manage.
Customers billed at zone price face a different (averaged) exposure than a generator paid at a single node.
caveats: The clearing price for power is uniform grid-wide, but this does NOT mean realized prices are uniform — congestion and losses make node/zone/hub prices diverge from that clearing price and from each other.
